plan: Complete enhanced-ACT humanities passage (CLD-P-ACT-R-000038, 'The Space Between Words'), about 600 words, on continuous script, the medieval Irish and British scribes who added word spaces, the historians' claim that spacing made silent reading ordinary, and skeptics' reading of the Augustine-Ambrose scene. Topic checked against every verbal bank passage (no word-spacing or silent-reading passage). 9 questions, 4 aimed at cross-paragraph inference or evidence evaluation.

passages.title: The Space Between Words
passages.text:
Imagine opening a book and finding every line printed like this: THEREADERHADTOFINDTHEWORDSHIMSELF. For much of ancient history, readers of Latin faced something close to that. Many manuscripts ran their letters together without spaces, a style scholars call continuous script. To a modern eye, a page written this way looks less like a text than like a puzzle.

It was not, for its first readers, as hard as it looks. Ancient readers very often read aloud, to themselves or to listeners, and a voice sounding out syllables could hear where one word ended and the next began even when the eye could not see it. A text in continuous script was in some ways closer to a musical score than to a modern page: it recorded sounds to be performed, and the performer supplied the breaks.

The spaces arrived from an unexpected direction. In the seventh and eighth centuries, scribes in Ireland and Britain, copying Latin texts in monasteries, began separating words with small gaps. For these scribes, Latin was not a native tongue but a learned one, and the boundaries that a Roman ear might have caught at once were not obvious to them. Spacing was a way of making a foreign language easier to read accurately. Some scribes added other aids as well, such as a larger letter at the start of a sentence, so that the page itself began to show readers how to divide it. Over the following centuries, the practice spread across Europe.

Some historians have argued that this small change had large consequences. With words already separated on the page, they suggest, a reader no longer needed to sound out a line to make sense of it; the eye could take in whole words at a glance. On this view, word spacing helped turn silent reading from an unusual skill into an ordinary habit, and with it came a more private, faster kind of reading.

Other scholars think this story exaggerates the change. They point out that ancient writers mention people reading silently without treating it as remarkable. The most famous evidence on the other side comes from Augustine, who described his surprise at seeing the bishop Ambrose read with his eyes moving and his voice silent. The scene is often cited as proof that silent reading was strange in the fourth century. Yet Augustine goes on to guess at Ambrose's reasons, perhaps to rest his voice or to avoid being drawn into discussions by listeners, which suggests that what surprised him was a public figure's choice, not an impossible feat.

Both sides may be partly right. Spaces did not invent silent reading, which some ancient readers clearly practiced. But a habit that is possible is not the same as a habit that is easy, and a page that does some of the reader's work can change who reads, and how, without anyone deciding that it should. The history of reading, in other words, is partly a history of what pages ask of the people who read them.

candidates.stem: Which of the following statements best expresses the main idea of the passage?

choices.A: Word spacing was invented so that monks could read silently without disturbing others.
choices.B: Spacing probably made silent reading easier and more common but did not create it.
choices.C: Ancient readers could not read silently until spaces were added between words.
choices.D: Continuous script was harder for ancient readers than it is for readers today.

candidates.evidence: Spaces did not invent silent reading
candidates.explanation: The passage presents a claim (spacing made silent reading common), a challenge (silent reading already existed), and a middle position: spacing did not invent silent reading but may have made it easier and more widespread.

A.rationale: The scribes added spaces to read a foreign language accurately, not to read silently.

C.rationale: The passage says some ancient readers 'clearly practiced' silent reading.

D.rationale: The passage says it was not as hard for its first readers as it looks to us.

hints: Where does the passage end up?

strategy.explanation: Use the last paragraph to weigh the two views.

candidates.remember: When a passage presents a debate, the main idea is often the author's resolution.

candidates.stem: The author begins the passage with a line printed without spaces mainly in order to:

choices.A: give modern readers a direct sense of what continuous script was like.
choices.B: show that ancient scribes made frequent errors when copying texts.
choices.C: prove that continuous script was impossible for anyone to read.
choices.D: suggest that modern books should return to continuous script.

candidates.evidence: For much of ancient history, readers of Latin faced something close to that.
candidates.explanation: The run-together line lets the reader experience continuous script before the author explains it, which sets up the contrast with how ancient readers handled it.

B.rationale: The line imitates a style, not a copying error.

C.rationale: The next paragraph says it was not as hard for ancient readers.

hints: What does the next sentence say the line resembles?

strategy.explanation: Ask what the example lets the reader experience.

candidates.remember: An opening example often lets readers feel a problem before it is explained.

candidates.stem: According to the passage, reading aloud made continuous script easier to read because:

choices.A: listeners could correct a reader who made a mistake.
choices.B: ancient readers memorized most texts before reading them.
choices.C: hearing the syllables helped a reader tell where each word ended.
choices.D: spoken Latin used fewer words than written Latin did.

candidates.evidence: a voice sounding out syllables could hear where one word ended and the next began
candidates.explanation: The voice could hear word boundaries 'even when the eye could not see' them, so reading aloud supplied the breaks the page lacked.

A.rationale: Listeners are mentioned, but not as correcting errors.

D.rationale: Nothing compares spoken and written Latin in this way.

hints: What could the voice do that the eye could not?

strategy.explanation: Find the sentence that explains why reading aloud helped.

candidates.remember: Look for 'even when' clauses that explain how a difficulty was overcome.

candidates.stem: The passage suggests that Irish and British scribes were more likely than Roman readers to need spaces between words because the scribes:

choices.A: copied texts more quickly than Roman readers needed to read them.
choices.B: were required by their monasteries to read only in silence.
choices.C: used a different alphabet from the one Roman readers used.
choices.D: knew Latin as a learned language rather than a native one.

candidates.evidence: the boundaries that a Roman ear might have caught at once were not obvious to them
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 2 explains that hearing a word's sounds let readers find its boundaries; paragraph 3 says Latin was 'a learned' language for the scribes, so those boundaries were 'not obvious to them.' Spaces made up for what their ears could not supply.

B.rationale: Nothing says monasteries required silent reading.

C.rationale: The scribes were copying Latin texts; no other alphabet is mentioned.

hints: Why could a Roman reader find word boundaries without spaces?
candidates.remember: Combine a general explanation with a specific case to infer a cause.

author_checklist.hardness: Students must connect paragraph 2's mechanism (the ear finds boundaries) to paragraph 3's non-native scribes; the 'required silence' choice tempts readers who expect the passage's later topic here.

candidates.stem: In paragraph 2, the comparison of a text in continuous script to "a musical score" mainly suggests that such a text:

choices.A: was meant to be performed aloud, with the reader adding the breaks.
choices.B: was decorated with musical symbols to guide its readers.
choices.C: was usually sung by its readers rather than spoken aloud.
choices.D: was written only for trained musicians to read aloud.

candidates.evidence: it recorded sounds to be performed, and the performer supplied the breaks
candidates.explanation: Like a score, the text recorded sounds to be performed, and the reader, like a performer, supplied what the page left out: the breaks between words.

B.rationale: The comparison concerns how the text was used, not decoration.

C.rationale: The comparison is about performance in general, not singing.

D.rationale: Nothing limits continuous script to musicians.

hints: What does the rest of the sentence say a score does?

strategy.explanation: Read the explanation after the colon.

candidates.remember: An author often explains a comparison right after making it.

candidates.stem: In paragraph 5, the skeptical scholars' point about Augustine's account of Ambrose is that the account:

choices.A: proves that silent reading was unknown before Ambrose's time.
choices.B: shows surprise at a choice, not at an impossible skill.
choices.C: was written long after Augustine had actually seen Ambrose.
choices.D: shows that Ambrose read aloud whenever he was in public.

candidates.evidence: which suggests that what surprised him was a public figure's choice, not an impossible feat
candidates.explanation: The skeptics note that Augustine guesses at Ambrose's reasons (resting his voice, avoiding discussion), which treats silent reading as a choice someone might make, so the surprise was about the choice, not about whether it could be done.

A.rationale: This is the reading the skeptics argue against.

C.rationale: The passage says nothing about when Augustine wrote it.

D.rationale: The scene shows Ambrose reading silently.

hints: Why does Augustine's guessing at reasons matter?
candidates.remember: The same evidence can support opposite readings; look for which detail each side uses.

author_checklist.hardness: Students must follow how the skeptics reinterpret a famous piece of evidence; the 'proves unknown' choice is the very reading being rejected.

candidates.stem: The author's position in the last paragraph is best described as:

choices.A: rejecting the historians' claim entirely in favor of the skeptics' view.
choices.B: dismissing the skeptics' evidence as too weak to change the conclusion.
choices.C: granting the skeptics' main point while keeping part of the historians' claim.
choices.D: declining to take a clear position on either side of the question.

candidates.evidence: Spaces did not invent silent reading, which some ancient readers clearly practiced.
candidates.explanation: The author agrees with the skeptics that silent reading existed before spacing, yet keeps the historians' idea that spacing changed reading by making silent reading easier and more common.

A.rationale: The author says spacing may still have changed 'who reads, and how.'

B.rationale: The author grants that some ancient readers 'clearly practiced' silent reading.

D.rationale: The author offers a clear middle position.

hints: Which side's claim does the author accept, and which part of the other side's claim does the author keep?

strategy.explanation: Split the last paragraph into what is granted and what is kept.

candidates.remember: A balanced conclusion grants one side's point while keeping part of the other's.

author_checklist.hardness: Students must separate what the author grants from what the author keeps; one-sided choices catch readers who notice only one sentence.

candidates.stem: Which of the following findings, if true, would most strengthen the skeptics' position described in paragraph 5?

choices.A: Monasteries that adopted word spacing produced more books each year.
choices.B: Modern readers read faster when words are separated by spaces.
choices.C: Irish scribes were the first in Europe to separate words with spaces.
choices.D: Many ordinary ancient letters mention silent reading without comment.

candidates.evidence: ancient writers mention people reading silently without treating it as remarkable
candidates.explanation: The skeptics argue silent reading was ordinary before spacing. More ancient accounts of silent reading treated as unremarkable would directly support that.

A.rationale: Book production does not bear on whether ancient readers read silently.

B.rationale: This supports the historians' claim that spacing eased reading.

C.rationale: This concerns who introduced spacing, not whether silent reading came before it.

hints: What do the skeptics claim about ancient silent reading?

strategy.explanation: Ask which choices even concern ancient silent reading.

candidates.remember: Evidence strengthens a claim when it matches the kind of evidence the claim rests on.

author_checklist.hardness: Students must match evidence to the right side; the 'modern readers read faster' choice supports the opposing view.

candidates.stem: The fourth paragraph mainly serves to:

choices.A: explain why Irish scribes chose to add spaces between words.
choices.B: present a claim that the passage then goes on to question.
choices.C: describe the evidence that silent reading was common in ancient times.
choices.D: summarize the author's final view of word spacing.

candidates.evidence: Some historians have argued that this small change had large consequences.
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 4 sets out the historians' claim that spacing made silent reading ordinary; paragraph 5 challenges it, and paragraph 6 weighs both.

A.rationale: The scribes' reasons are given in paragraph 3.

C.rationale: That evidence comes in paragraph 5, from the skeptics.

D.rationale: The author's view comes in the last paragraph.

hints: What happens to the claim in paragraph 5?

strategy.explanation: Place paragraph 4 in the passage's structure.

candidates.remember: A paragraph that begins 'Some historians have argued' often sets up a counterargument.
